##Testing the output from test set

This chunk calculates goal error, compare against the training baseline and evaluate the predicted ranking:

```{r}
test_data$PredHomeGoalMean <- predict(home_selected_model, newdata = test_data, type = "response")
test_data$PredAwayGoalMean <- predict(away_selected_model, newdata = test_data, type = "response")

MAE_HG <- mean(abs(test_data$FTHG - test_data$PredHomeGoalMean))
MAE_AG <- mean(abs(test_data$FTAG - test_data$PredAwayGoalMean))
train_MAE_HG <- mean(abs(test_data$FTHG - mean(train_data$FTHG)))
train_MAE_AG <- mean(abs(test_data$FTAG - mean(train_data$FTAG)))
MAE_pos <- mean(abs(table_comparison$PositionDifference))
rank_corr <- cor(table_comparison$Position_Predicted,table_comparison$Position_Actual,method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")

print(c(MAE_HG, MAE_AG, train_MAE_HG, train_MAE_AG, MAE_pos, rank_corr))
```
These results taht the model performs better than the training baseline.
- Home goal MAE: 0.953 goals, compared with 0.996 for the baseline so a 4.3% reduction.
- Away goal MAE: 0.846 goals, compared with 0.875 for the baseline so a 3.3% reduction.
- Mean position error: 2.1 places. On average, a team’s predicted position was about two places away from its actual position.
- Spearman rank correlation: 0.862, indicating the predicted and actual league orders were fairly similar.
The model improved goal predictions over the baseline and reproduced the overall team ranking reasonably well on the test season.

## Why GLM?

The response variables (home goals and away goals) are non negative counts. A Poisson GLM models counts and uses a log link, so it predicts a positive expected goal rate, $\lambda$. The Poisson assumption also implies that the conditional mean and variance are equal.

Football-score research has used separate Poisson models for home and away goals as a baseline. More advanced models can account for dependence between the two scores, so Poisson is a defensible starting point, not a claim that it is the best possible model. Maher (1982)

Your own checks give you some support for it: the Pearson dispersion ratios were close to 1. Your test-season MAEs were also lower than the training-average baseline, although only modestly: about 0.953 versus 0.996 home goals, and 0.846 versus 0.875 away goals.

A concise way to present the choice:
I use separate Poisson GLMs for home and away goals because goals are count outcomes, and the log link gives positive expected goal counts. I use previous-match statistics as predictors and assess the models on a later season. The dispersion checks and baseline comparison make Poisson a reasonable starting point, while leaving room to compare it with more complex models.

##Questions

Why use a Poisson model instead of linear regression?
A linear model can predict negative or fractional goals. A Poisson GLM is designed for non-negative count outcomes and returns an expected goal rate.

What assumptions does Poisson make?
It assumes that, conditional on the predictors, goal-count variance equals the expected goal count. Your dispersion ratios are close to 1, which is encouraging, though it doesn’t prove every assumption holds.

Why fit separate home-goal and away-goal models?
Home and away scoring may behave differently. Separate models let each side have different predictor effects and expected goal rates.

How do you prevent information from the match being predicted leaking into the predictors?
The predictors should contain only information known before kickoff. Your “before” features are intended to do this; the current match’s result and statistics must not be included.

How did you test whether the model predicts well?
You trained on earlier seasons and evaluated on the later test season. The model modestly beat a baseline that always predicts the training-set average. You can also compare the predicted and actual final tables.

Does your model use the first months of 2026/27 to refit its coefficients?
In the code you showed, final_train_data combines train_data and test_data only. So the 2026/27 played matches are not used to refit the model coefficients. They can inform future predictions through the pre-match features if those features are updated using those results.

Does the current prediction code update each team’s form after every predicted fixture?
No. It predicts all remaining fixtures using the feature values already in prediction_data; it doesn’t add each forecast result to the inputs for the next fixture.

Are the predicted goal values actual predicted scores?
predict(..., type = "response") returns expected goals, \(\hat{\lambda}\), which can be decimal values. Your table function compares them as though they were scores. That can produce implausible win/draw points—two expected-goal values are rarely exactly equal, so draws may be undercounted. Before presenting the league-table method, decide whether to round forecasts or use score probabilities or simulations to derive match outcomes.

How do you handle teams with little Premier League history?
Their early-season predictors are based on less information, so their forecasts are less reliable. Coventry is one example in your data. State this as a limitation.

The last two questions are the most important to resolve before presenting your predicted 2026/27 table: the current code doesn’t recursively update future features, and it treats expected goals as if they were match scores.
